predictions.text: The thing is though Iroh never really went through any great trials or struggle for redemption in the show. By the time we see him he’s essentially already finished 90% of his redemption arc and all that’s left is for him to atone for his actions, which he does in the series finale without hesitation or character development. Hell, he never even expresses guilt for his past actions outside of his son’s death and the only time anyone calls him out for his past is a no name earth kingdom soldier whose framed as unsympathetic and antagonistic. That’s why there’s such a disconnect and why people constantly bring him up in relation to Azula. We only ever see Iroh post the majority of his redemption arc and are only ever vaguely told about what he needs to redeem himself for, while with Azula we are only shown her while she is still young and has yet to reach the point to want to redeem herself. So it’s really easy to accept Iroh’s redemption at face value when we don’t ever see him being evil, while it’s really easy to not accept the possibility of Azula ever being able to redeem herself when we have only ever seen her when she’s evil. But logically speaking if it’s possible for Iroh to eventually find redemption after spending decades committing atrocities and leading the Fire Nation on the frontlines, then it should also be possible for Azula to eventually recognize the error of her ways and begin the path towards redemption.

As other people have pointed out in this very thread, the overwhelming majority of fans see shipping as annoying nonsense. And for the most part it is. I remember what Gene Roddenberry said about Star Trek's fan discourse. Which basically boils down to, "If we did everything the fans wanted the show would suck." And he was right, and that applies to everything. More than that storylines and pairings are played with, discussed and discarded ALL THE TIME. They are not locked in to decisions they made nearly two decades ago. For the record, I'm not saying you're wrong, it's just people should be prepared for the possibility. Because writers can and do change their minds. Which was the whole point of this entire thread, to get people to acknowledge the possibility that they're storytelling choices have changed have changed over almost twenty years.

I appreciate the point about looking "beyond the frame." My "muddied" comment isn't about silencing perspectives — it’s about maintaining logical consistency. If I call a character "polite," and someone argues, "No, he's rude because he doesn't take his shoes off in the house," they are importing an external cultural rule the story never established. They aren't analyzing the character's behavior; they are penalizing the character for failing to meet an outside standard. We can all agree Iroh was part of a horrific, imperialist machine. That is a moral judgment we make through our modern lens, and it’s 100% valid. But "War Criminal" is a technical classification. This raises two questions: *1. "Was Iroh simply not taking his sandals off?" If we decide "General of an unjust war = War Criminal," we create a blanket rule that makes every soldier who fought for the "wrong side" a criminal, regardless of their conduct. This actually weakens the moral critique. If everyone is a war criminal, the term no longer describes someone who commits atrocities—it just describes someone who lost an unjust war. *2. Does the narrative need Iroh to wear the sandals inside the house? I think Iroh’s arc is more powerful if he wasn't an atrocity-committer. If he’s a "war criminal," his story is a simple "Bad Guy turns Good." But if he was an honorable, disciplined, "good man" who was a high-functioning tool for a system of pure destruction, the story is a tragedy. It’s about a good soldier for an evil cause realizing his entire worldview was a lie. When we force the "criminal" label on him without textual evidence of a specific crime, we flatten that nuance. You don’t need Iroh to be a criminal to recognize that his past was a tragedy that required a lifetime of atonement.

Personally, i have absolutely no problem with Zuko and Mai never getting back together, or Sokka and Suki not working out. I hate it when stories about children/young adults end up with them all paired off with each other and then they stay that way. It just makes the world feel so small and empty and childish. Kids form crushes and then move on in a matter of months all the time irl, it’s actually pretty rare for relationships between high schoolers to genuinely work out long term. These kids are world travelers, the LEADERS of their generation. You’re trying to tell me that they never formed healthy, adult relationships with anyone new? Not ONE of them?
But this isn't real life. This is a cartoon, it's not random genetics it's intentional design.

I disagree from a writing/technical standpoint, because after reading the Iroh comic I'm fairly sure Iroh is simply not meant to have a messy past. He is supposed to have a tragic past, not a messy one, but the writers accidentally went a wee bit too far with it.

For me it isnt about measure in morality or capacity for remorse. It is if the right conditions are presented for a character to change or at least question their way of thinking. Its all about possibility. Sometimes when an Azula's redemption is being discussed one of the opposing argument is that Iroh changed into a better man or that he regreted, but this actually reinforces Azula's chances. Iroh was a respectable general that served with no regrets his nation and after a personal loss changed his ways, and he was an adult in his 40~50. The circunstances made him change. Its entirely plausible using him as an exemple, because Iroh and Azula actually have many points in common.
